narrationPlan.voice: One clear, warm narrator throughout; no character voices
narrationPlan.pace: Calm, clear, and curious (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a single narrator: this is a science article, not a story with characters.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Say numbers and units in full ("one hundred and fifty million kilometres", "astronomical units") and pronounce names clearly.

teacherGuide.overview: Teaches the three states of matter and the particle model through Ghanaian examples, extends changes of state to molten rock and the role of pressure, and links melting ice to volcanoes abroad and to sea-level rise on Ghana’s coast.
learningGoals: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in solids, liquids, and gases.
Name the changes of state and state the melting and boiling points of water.
Explain how pressure, as well as temperature, affects whether a material is solid or liquid.
Explain the greenhouse effect and one way that global warming affects Ghana.

beforeReading: Ask learners to name three solids, three liquids, and three gases found in the school compound.
whileReading: Pause on Page 2 and have groups of learners act as particles in a solid, a liquid, and a gas.
afterReading: Place one ice cube in the sun and one in the shade; time each as it melts and explain the difference.
discussion: Shea butter, toothpaste, and gari soaked in water: is each a solid or a liquid? Why are some materials hard to classify?
reflection: What signs of a changing climate have older people in your community noticed?

mathsExtension.task: It takes about 334 joules of heat to melt 1 gram of ice at 0 °C. How much heat is needed to melt a 500 g block?
Rock melts at about 1,000 °C and water boils at 100 °C. How many times greater is the melting temperature of rock, in degrees Celsius?

support: Give a diagram of the changes of state with the arrows drawn and the names left blank for learners to fill in.
stretch: Find out why a pressure cooker cooks food faster, and why water boils below 100 °C on a very high mountain.

factCheck.claim: Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at standard pressure; the latent heat of fusion of ice is about 334 J/g; the April 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption in Iceland disrupted European air travel.
factCheck.explanation: Post-glacial decompression melting in Iceland (~12,000 years ago) is well established in geology, while modern glacier retreat effects on volcanic activity remain under active study.
factCheck.reference: Smithsonian Institution Global Volcanism Program; Jull & McKenzie (1996), Journal of Geophysical Research.
